disclaimer: Typical adult reference ranges; labs vary; not for clinical decisions.

sources.guyton13: Hall JE. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 13th edition. Philadelphia: Elsevier; 2016.

values.label: Synaptic gap (synaptic space) width
values.where: Chapter 7, Excitation of Skeletal Muscle: Neuromuscular Transmission and Excitation-Contraction Coupling: 'Physiologic Anatomy of the Neuromuscular Junction—The Motor End Plate' (the space between the terminal and the fiber membrane, the synaptic space or synaptic cleft, is 20 to 30 nanometers wide).
values.note: Anatomy only: the teaching model does not change the width of the gap.

values.label: Acetylcholine vesicles released per nerve impulse
values.where: Chapter 7: 'Secretion of Acetylcholine by the Nerve Terminals' (when a nerve impulse reaches the neuromuscular junction, about 125 vesicles of acetylcholine are released from the terminals into the synaptic space).
values.note: The source gives a single approximate value, not a range.

values.label: End plate potential, size of the rise
values.where: Chapter 7: 'End Plate Potential and Excitation of the Skeletal Muscle Fiber', page 91 (sodium entering when the channels open makes the potential inside the fiber at the end plate increase in the positive direction as much as 50 to 75 millivolts, creating a local potential called the end plate potential).

values.label: Safety factor: end plate potential compared with the amount needed to fire the fibre
values.where: Chapter 7: 'Safety Factor for Transmission at the Neuromuscular Junction; Fatigue of the Junction' (ordinarily, each impulse that arrives at the neuromuscular junction causes about three times as much end plate potential as that required to stimulate the muscle fiber).
values.note: The source gives a single approximate value, not a range. The model reports the average over its fibres.

values.label: Skeletal muscle fibre, resting membrane potential
values.where: Chapter 7: 'Muscle Action Potential' (resting membrane potential: about -80 to -90 millivolts in skeletal fibers, the same as in large myelinated nerve fibers).
values.note: The model reads the membrane right beside the end plate; only the model's succinylcholine slider moves it.

values.label: Skeletal muscle action potential, duration
values.where: Chapter 7: 'Muscle Action Potential' (duration of action potential: 1 to 5 milliseconds in skeletal muscle, about five times as long as in large myelinated nerves).
values.note: Shown for reference: the teaching model does not simulate the shape of the muscle action potential.

values.label: Skeletal muscle action potential, conduction velocity
values.where: Chapter 7: 'Muscle Action Potential' (velocity of conduction: 3 to 5 m/sec, about 1/13 the velocity of conduction in the large myelinated nerve fibers that excite skeletal muscle).
values.note: Shown for reference: the teaching model does not simulate how fast the wave travels.

states.label: Nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockers (curariform drugs)
states.summary: They occupy the acetylcholine receptors without opening them, so acetylcholine cannot open enough channels and the end plate potential no longer reaches the level needed to fire the muscle fibre.
states.where: Chapter 7: 'Drugs That Block Transmission at the Neuromuscular Junction' (curariform drugs such as D-tubocurarine block the action of acetylcholine on the muscle fiber acetylcholine receptors, preventing sufficient increase in permeability of the muscle membrane channels to initiate an action potential: a smaller end plate potential, below what is required, so the safety factor falls).
states.modelNote: The model shows a moderate block: about a quarter of fibres miss on the first impulse and most miss by the end of a quick burst.

states.label: Cholinesterase inhibitors (reversal)
states.summary: They stop acetylcholinesterase breaking acetylcholine down, so more acetylcholine builds up in the gap with each impulse and acts on the receptors for longer.
states.where: Chapter 7: 'Drugs That Stimulate the Neuromuscular Junction by Inactivating Acetylcholinesterase' (neostigmine, physostigmine and diisopropyl fluorophosphate inactivate the acetylcholinesterase in the synapses, so with each successive nerve impulse additional acetylcholine accumulates and stimulates the muscle fiber: more acetylcholine acting on the receptors, end plate potential up). Chapter 7: 'Myasthenia Gravis Causes Muscle Weakness' (an anticholinesterase drug allows larger than normal amounts of acetylcholine to accumulate in the synaptic space).
states.modelNote: Selecting this state shows the inhibitor on its own. To see a reversal, move the blocker slider up first, then turn cholinesterase down.

states.label: Myasthenia gravis
states.summary: Antibodies block or destroy the muscle's own acetylcholine receptors, so the end plate potentials are mostly too weak to fire the muscle fibre and the muscles are weak.
states.where: Chapter 7: 'Myasthenia Gravis Causes Muscle Weakness' (antibodies block or destroy the acetylcholine receptors at the postsynaptic neuromuscular junction; the end plate potentials that occur in the muscle fibers are mostly too weak to initiate opening of the voltage-gated sodium channels, so muscle fiber depolarization does not occur).
states.modelNote: The model shows myasthenia gravis as a fifth of the normal receptors remaining.

states.label: Fatigue of the junction (very rapid, prolonged nerve firing)
states.summary: Firing the nerve very fast for minutes uses up acetylcholine vesicles faster than the nerve ending can refill them, so fewer are released per impulse and impulses start failing to pass to the muscle.
states.where: Chapter 7: 'Safety Factor for Transmission at the Neuromuscular Junction; Fatigue of the Junction' (stimulation of the nerve fiber at rates greater than 100 times per second for several minutes often diminishes the number of acetylcholine vesicles so much that impulses fail to pass into the muscle fiber).
states.modelNote: The model shows fatigue as a tenth of the normal release per impulse.
